newsitem.title: UK: Highland sees tough UK market,improving U.S..
newsitem.headline: Highland sees tough UK market,improving U.S..

text.p: Whisky-maker Highland Distilleries Plc, owners of the blend Famous Grouse, said on Tuesday conditions in Britain remain very difficult, with sales volumes continuing to contract.
But in an interview chief executive Brian Ivory said he thinks the market for spirits in North America has finally turned a corner after a decade in the doldrums.

The company reported a 12 percent increase in its pre-tax profit for the half-year to February 28 to 24.9 million pounds, in line with stockmarket forecasts. The shares slipped 1-1/2 pence to 342-1/2p by 1125 GMT.

The company included for the first time prestigious single malt whisky producer Macallan-Glenlivet for a full period. Macallan posted a profit of 5.0 million pounds but this was offset by the cost of financing the acquisition, which produced an interest bill of two million pounds.
A rise in the value of the pound adversely affected Highland's results by around one million pound.
Sales overseas of the Famous Grouse grew five percent on a like for like basis in the six month period, the company said.
The main increases were in Greece, Holland and Sweden while France was disappointing but exports to North America and Asia showed strong growth.
In Britain industry sales were down by five percent in the period.
"I think European economies will continue to find the going tough in trying to fit into the Maastricht corset in the run up to a single currency," said Ivory.
"But I think we will see growth in continental Europe albeit against the background of a difficult market."
Macallan suffered from heavy price competition over the critical Christmas period.
"Some brands were five pounds cheaper in December than in October. Macallan was two pounds fifty cheaper, so sales were down slightly," said Ivory.
Highland refused to take part in the heavy promotional activity and price discounting offered by its competitors.
In North America exports of Famous Grouse rose 19 percent in the period and sales of single malt Macallan were up 20 percent, the strongest increase in sales to the region for a decade, said Ivory.
"I think the market for spirits in North America probably has turned a corner, but how sharp the corner and how steep the trend I am not sure."
"Certainly the demand for Scotch and the image of Scotch has improved, it is now considered a prestigious product again."
Ivory said the company expects to achieve an overall 1997 price increase of about two percent on its brands overseas.
In Britain Highland announced a price rise of just over four percent, which comes into effect in mid-April, on its leading brand Famous Grouse.
"Our assessment of the market is that we feel it will stick," said Ivory.
A litre bottle of Famous Grouse costs about 16.09 pounds at supermarket chain ASDA Group Plc, against Asda's own brand at 8.69 pounds and Teachers at 11.69 pounds.
